Yo lo vendería así:

> **Cala FastPath convierte una pregunta de negocio en una consulta Cala validada. Si no puede hacerlo con seguridad, no la ejecuta.**

No empieces hablando de GLiNER2, LoRA o Pioneer. Eso explica cómo lo construiste, pero no por qué debería importar.

### Pitch de 45 segundos

> Hoy, usar Cala Knowledge Query exige conocer su sintaxis. Podemos poner un modelo grande delante, pero cada consulta añade latencia, coste y resultados difíciles de controlar.
>
> Cala FastPath toma lenguaje natural, genera un plan estructurado, lo valida y lo compila a Cala QL. Cala sigue siendo quien ejecuta la consulta. Si falta información o la petición no es segura, FastPath se detiene.
>
> La hipótesis es que un modelo pequeño, entrenado para este contrato concreto, puede resolver las consultas habituales con menos latencia y coste que un modelo generalista. Y no queremos demostrarlo con una demo preparada: hemos construido un benchmark reproducible y un holdout sellado para medir precisión y cobertura.

La frase clave es:

> **No reemplazamos Cala. Hacemos que más gente pueda usarlo correctamente.**

### Cómo haría la demo

1. Enseña una consulta Cala QL para dejar claro el problema:
   `startups.location=Spain.funding>10M.funding<50M.return(name,funding)`

2. Activa FastPath y escribe:
   > Spanish startups with funding between 10M and 50M

3. Muestra el recorrido visible:
   > lenguaje natural → plan → Cala QL → resultado de Cala

4. Ejecuta otra con composición:
   > Top 5 Spanish startups by funding

5. Termina con una consulta fuera de alcance. FastPath debe abstenerse y no llamar a Cala. Ese fallo controlado es uno de los mejores argumentos del proyecto.

La demo debería durar unos 90 segundos. Una consulta simple, una compleja y una abstención.

### Qué estás vendiendo realmente

| No lo presentes como | Preséntalo como |
|---|---|
| “Hemos entrenado un LoRA” | “Hemos creado una vía rápida para las consultas frecuentes de Cala” |
| “Un chatbot para Cala” | “Un compilador controlado de lenguaje natural a Cala QL” |
| “Entiende cualquier pregunta” | “Ejecuta lo que puede validar y rechaza el resto” |
| “Es más rápido y barato” | “Vamos a medir si mantiene precisión reduciendo latencia y coste” |

### Estructura de una presentación de 5 minutos

1. **El problema:** Cala es potente, pero su sintaxis limita quién puede usarlo.
2. **El producto:** lenguaje natural dentro de la interfaz actual de Cala.
3. **La diferencia:** plan tipado, validación, compilación y abstención.
4. **La demo:** éxito, composición y rechazo seguro.
5. **La evidencia:** SOTA contra GLiNER2 base y GLiNER2 LoRA sobre el mismo contrato.
6. **El cierre:** integrar el modelo real y medirlo en el holdout sellado.

### Importante para no sobrevenderlo

Ahora mismo, el repositorio demuestra bien la arquitectura, la extensión, el compilador y la metodología de evaluación. Pero la interfaz utiliza un **“Mock SLM”** con tres consultas configuradas, y no veo resultados acreditados de un LoRA entrenado. Hay 21 ejemplos de entrenamiento y un holdout sellado de 40 casos.

Por tanto, hoy lo presentaría como:

> **Un prototipo de producto funcional y una hipótesis técnica preparada para ser medida.**

No como un modelo terminado ni como una mejora de velocidad o precisión ya demostrada. Esa honestidad juega a favor en un hackathon: el proyecto no es solo una demo bonita, también tiene una forma seria de comprobar si funciona.

La narrativa técnica completa ya está bien definida en [demo.md](C:\Users\vrosciano\Documents\ChatGPT\hackaton\demo.md) y el estado de la integración está descrito en [extension/README.md](C:\Users\vrosciano\Documents\ChatGPT\hackaton\extension\README.md).

I’ll translate it into natural presentation English, keeping the claims appropriately cautious. I’m applying `unslop` so it sounds spoken rather than like corporate pitch copy.

I’d position it like this:

> **Cala FastPath turns a business question into a validated Cala query. If it cannot do so safely, it does not run the query.**

Do not open with GLiNER2, LoRA, or Pioneer. Those explain how you built it, not why anyone should care.

### 45-second pitch

> Today, using Cala Knowledge Query requires users to understand its query language. We could put a large language model in front of it, but that adds latency, cost, and less predictable results to every query.
>
> Cala FastPath takes a natural-language request, creates a structured plan, validates it, and compiles it into Cala QL. Cala still executes the query. If the request is incomplete or unsafe, FastPath stops before calling Cala.
>
> Our hypothesis is that a small model trained for this specific contract can handle common queries with lower latency and cost than a general-purpose model. We are not relying on a prepared demo to prove that. We built a reproducible benchmark and a sealed holdout to measure accuracy and coverage.

The key line is:

> **We are not replacing Cala. We are making it easier for more people to use Cala correctly.**

### How I would run the demo

1. Show a Cala QL query to establish the problem:

   `startups.location=Spain.funding>10M.funding<50M.return(name,funding)`

2. Enable FastPath and type:

   > Spanish startups with funding between 10M and 50M

3. Show the visible flow:

   > Natural language → structured plan → Cala QL → Cala result

4. Run a more complex request:

   > Top 5 Spanish startups by funding

5. Finish with an unsupported request. FastPath should abstain and avoid calling Cala. That controlled failure is one of the strongest parts of the project.

Keep the live demo under 90 seconds. Show one straightforward query, one composed query, and one safe rejection.

### What you are really selling

| Avoid saying | Say instead |
|---|---|
| “We trained a LoRA” | “We built a fast path for common Cala queries” |
| “It is a chatbot for Cala” | “It is a controlled compiler from natural language to Cala QL” |
| “It understands any question” | “It runs what it can validate and rejects the rest” |
| “It is faster and cheaper” | “We are measuring whether it can preserve accuracy while reducing latency and cost” |

### Five-minute presentation structure

1. **The problem.** Cala is powerful, but its query language limits who can use it.
2. **The product.** Natural-language queries inside Cala’s existing interface.
3. **What makes it different.** A typed plan, validation, compilation, and safe abstention.
4. **The demo.** A successful query, a composed query, and a controlled rejection.
5. **The evidence.** The same contract compares a frontier model, base GLiNER2, and the fine-tuned GLiNER2 model.
6. **The next step.** Connect the trained model and run the sealed holdout.

### Be honest about the current state

The repository already demonstrates the architecture, browser integration, compiler, and evaluation method. However, the current interface uses a **“Mock SLM”** with three configured queries, and the repository does not contain verified results from a trained LoRA model.

The project currently has 21 training examples and a sealed holdout containing 40 cases.

So today, I would describe it as:

> **A working product prototype with a technical hypothesis that is ready to be measured.**

I would not describe it as a finished model or claim proven speed, cost, or accuracy improvements yet. That honesty helps the pitch. You have built more than a polished demo. You have also built a credible way to test whether the idea works.

Hay una corrección importante: lo que aparece en este proyecto es ajuste LoRA para extracción estructurada, no RL en sentido estricto. Voy a redactarlo sin quitar mérito a la curva de aprendizaje. También comprobaré cómo describir Luna con precisión y aplicaré `unslop` para que el texto siga sonando a ti, no a marketing genérico.

Sí. El mejor ángulo es presentar el proyecto como un experimento técnico serio, no como si el modelo actual ya compitiera con GPT.

Una precisión: no diría que es tu primera vez haciendo “RL”. El repositorio muestra fine-tuning con LoRA para extracción estructurada, no reinforcement learning. Di que es tu primera experiencia entrenando y ajustando un modelo, trabajando con LoRA y usando Pioneer.

### Technical pitch in English

> At first glance, Cala FastPath looks like a natural-language interface for Cala. But the real question behind the project is more technical:
>
> Can a small, specialized language model replace a much larger general-purpose model for a narrow and structured query task?
>
> The pipeline uses GLiNER2 as a small language model for NER-style information extraction and classification. It extracts spans such as company names, locations, funding amounts, and limits. It also classifies the query root, requested fields, sort order, and whether the request is supported.
>
> The model does not generate or execute Cala QL directly. It produces a typed intermediate plan. We validate that plan and pass it through a deterministic compiler that generates the final Cala query. Cala remains responsible for execution.
>
> This separation is important. It lets us identify whether a failure came from entity extraction, intent classification, plan validation, compilation, or Cala itself. It also allows FastPath to abstain when the model is not confident enough, instead of sending a potentially unsafe query.
>
> This demo uses a small number of controlled examples. The current SLM is far less capable than a model such as GPT-5.6 Luna. Luna is already designed for cost-sensitive, high-volume workloads, so it is a demanding baseline rather than an artificially expensive comparison. [OpenAI currently lists Luna at $0.20 per million input tokens and $1.20 per million output tokens.](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-5.6-luna)
>
> I am not claiming that this prototype beats Luna today. The demo proves that the architecture works. It shows that natural language can be converted into a constrained, inspectable, and executable Cala query using a small specialized model.
>
> With a larger team and more time, we could build a much broader annotated dataset, add difficult negative examples, improve multilingual coverage, calibrate confidence thresholds, and iterate on the LoRA training. We could then measure accuracy, coverage, latency, and cost on a genuinely unseen benchmark.
>
> For me, this was also a significant learning project. It was my first time fine-tuning a model with LoRA and using the Pioneer platform. The hardest part was not simply training the model. I had to understand Pioneer’s data contract, convert the dataset into exact-span extraction tasks, design the intermediate schema, build the validator and compiler, and integrate the whole flow into Cala’s existing interface.
>
> That integration took considerably more work than I expected, but it also taught me why the model is only one part of a reliable AI product. The dataset, contracts, validation, evaluation, and product integration matter just as much.
>
> So the result of the hackathon is not a production-ready model. It is a working technical prototype, an end-to-end training and evaluation pipeline, and a clear path for testing whether a specialized SLM can become a faster and cheaper query layer for Cala.

### Architecture line for a slide

```text
Natural language
      ↓
NER + classification with GLiNER2
      ↓
Typed query plan
      ↓
Validation and confidence policy
      ↓
Deterministic Cala QL compiler
      ↓
Cala execution
```

### Strong closing line

> **The demo is controlled, but the architecture is real. The next question is no longer whether this can be built. It is how far the specialized model can be pushed with better data, more training, and rigorous evaluation.**

I would avoid “the SLM is inferior.” A better technical formulation is:

> **The SLM has much less general reasoning capability, but it is optimized for a narrower extraction task.**

That sounds more accurate and makes the experiment compelling: you are testing whether specialization can compensate for model size.

Natural language
      ↓
NER + classification with GLiNER2

Typed query plan

Validation and confidence policy

## Presentation script

> Hi, I’m Vincenzo, and this is Cala FastPath.
>
> The idea started with a simple problem. Cala has a powerful Knowledge Query endpoint, but users need to understand Cala QL to use it correctly.
>
> I wanted to test whether users could describe the data they need in natural language, while Cala would continue receiving a valid and controlled Cala QL query.
>
> Instead of placing a general-purpose LLM directly in front of Cala, I explored a smaller and more specialized model.
>
> Cala FastPath uses GLiNER2 for two related tasks.
>
> The first is classification. The model identifies the operation, the root collection, the requested return fields, sorting instructions, and whether the request is supported.
>
> The second is NER, or named entity recognition. The model extracts exact spans from the request, such as “Google,” “Spain,” “10M,” or a result limit such as “5.”
>
> The result is a typed intermediate query plan.
>
> That distinction matters because the model does not write or execute Cala QL directly. The probabilistic part of the system ends at the typed plan.
>
> The plan then passes through validation and a confidence policy. If it is accepted, a deterministic compiler converts it into Cala QL. Cala executes the final query using its existing endpoint.
>
> If the plan is incomplete, invalid, or unsupported, FastPath stops. It does not send a speculative query to Cala.
>
> The complete pipeline looks like this.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Natural language"] --> B["GLiNER2"]
    B --> B1["Classification"]
    B --> B2["NER and span extraction"]
    B1 --> C["Typed query plan"]
    B2 --> C
    C --> D["Validation and confidence policy"]
    D --> E{"Accepted?"}
    E -- Yes --> F["Deterministic Cala QL compiler"]
    F --> G["Cala execution"]
    E -- No --> H["Safe abstention"]
```

> From the product side, FastPath could live directly inside Cala’s existing Knowledge Query interface.
>
> The user would switch between Cala QL and FastPath. In FastPath mode, they could write something like “Top five Spanish startups by funding.”
>
> FastPath would show the generated Cala QL, the structured plan, the model’s decision, and its latency. Cala would then display the result normally and keep the existing result URL and recent-query history.
>
> This means FastPath would not replace Cala’s query engine or introduce a separate execution path. It would make the existing Cala capability accessible to people who do not know its query language.
>
> It could also make common queries faster and cheaper than sending every request to a general-purpose model. More importantly, it would make the process inspectable. We can see what the model extracted, what the compiler generated, and where a failure occurred.
>
> I want to be clear about the current demo. It uses a small number of controlled examples, and the current SLM is much less capable than GPT-5.6 Luna.
>
> Luna is already one of OpenAI’s models for cost-sensitive, high-volume workloads. That makes it a strong baseline. I am not claiming that this prototype beats Luna today. The demo proves that the pipeline and the product integration work.
>
> With a larger team and more time, we could create a broader annotated dataset, add harder negative cases, cover more languages and query combinations, calibrate confidence thresholds, and run several LoRA training iterations.
>
> We could then compare the specialized model against Luna using the same typed-plan contract and measure exact-plan accuracy, coverage, unsafe acceptances, latency, and cost.
>
> Pioneer was one of the hardest parts of the project for me.
>
> This was my first time fine-tuning a model with LoRA and my first time using a training platform like Pioneer.
>
> My initial assumption was that I could train the model to generate the complete nested query structure directly. In practice, Pioneer and GLiNER2 required me to separate the problem into classification labels and NER annotations.
>
> The NER annotations also needed exact text spans and character offsets. If the request contained “10M,” the training data had to point to those exact characters. The model extracts “10M,” while the deterministic compiler decides that it represents a funding filter.
>
> That forced me to redesign the dataset format and clarify the boundary between the model and the compiler.
>
> I also had to build the complete integration around the training process. This included dataset conversion, local validation against GLiNER2’s native format, dataset uploads through signed URLs, job polling, training diagnostics, and evaluation.
>
> I spent more time on data contracts, validation, and integration than on the actual training call. That was probably the most valuable lesson from the project.
>
> Training a model is only one part of building a reliable AI feature. The difficult part is defining exactly what the model should produce, checking that output, measuring failures, and connecting it safely to a real product.
>
> Cala FastPath is still a technical prototype. But it demonstrates the full path from natural language to a controlled Cala execution, and it gives us a concrete way to test whether a specialized SLM can become a useful query layer for Cala.

## Strong final line

> **The model in this demo is small and the examples are controlled, but the architecture is real. The next step is to find out how far specialization, better data, and rigorous evaluation can take it.**

Eso fortalece la parte personal. Yo reemplazaría la sección de Pioneer por esta:

> Pioneer was one of the hardest parts of the project.
>
> This was my first time fine-tuning a model with LoRA and working with a model-training platform. Some of Pioneer’s endpoints and data contracts took time to understand and integrate. I had to work through dataset uploads, signed URLs, validation formats, training jobs, status polling, logs, and inference.
>
> I also discovered that the format I had designed initially did not match how GLiNER2 expected the task to be represented. I had to separate the problem into classification labels and NER annotations with exact text spans and character offsets.
>
> Since I could not rely entirely on the remote training workflow, I also made an effort to train and test the model locally. I managed to improve its behavior compared with the base model, which showed that the approach had potential.
>
> However, local training quickly reached the limits of my computer. I did not have enough compute and memory to run larger datasets, longer experiments, or several training iterations.
>
> So the current result should be understood as a constrained prototype. With more compute, more training data, and a larger team, the same approach could be tested much more seriously. We could run several LoRA configurations, analyze errors, calibrate confidence thresholds, and measure the final model against the sealed benchmark.
>
> This experience also changed how I think about model training. The training command itself was a small part of the work. Most of the effort went into understanding the platform, designing the dataset correctly, validating the output, and connecting the model safely to Cala.

Una buena transición hacia el cierre sería:

> **I reached the limits of my hardware, not the limits of the idea.**

Y después:

> The demo is small and controlled, but it proves that the full pipeline can work. The next step is to give it the data, compute, and engineering time needed to find out how far it can go.

No afirmaría que la mejora local fue “significant” salvo que tengas métricas. “I managed to improve its behavior compared with the base model” transmite el avance sin inventar una cifra.

Voy a condensarlo en un guion hablado en inglés de unas 170 palabras, aproximadamente 75–85 segundos. Corregiré “SML” a “SLM” y dejaré la limitación de los tres ejemplos completamente explícita. Aplicaré `unslop` para que resulte cómodo de leer en voz alta.

Aproximadamente 1 minuto y 20 segundos:

> Hi, I’m Vincenzo, and this is Cala FastPath.
>
> This project explores how a small language model can help Cala understand what the user actually wants before building a query.
>
> Sometimes a Cala query returns more information than the user needs. This becomes harder with longer, more complex requests because every field, filter, or relationship creates another place where the query can go wrong.
>
> FastPath uses an SLM trained through Pioneer. It combines intent classification and NER to identify the requested entities, filters, fields, ordering, and limits.
>
> The model produces a typed query plan. A deterministic compiler validates that plan and converts it into a more specific Cala QL query. Cala then executes it normally.
>
> I connected this flow to Cala through a Chrome extension, so FastPath appears directly inside the existing Knowledge Query interface.
>
> Today’s demo is deliberately controlled and supports three examples. It proves the integration and the pipeline, not that the model is production-ready.
>
> Pioneer was challenging because I had to understand its endpoints, training formats, and exact NER annotations. I also trained the model locally and saw some improvements, but my computer could not support larger experiments.
>
> With more data, compute, and engineering time, this approach could be tested against much more complex Cala queries.
